Mindfulness and tDCS Paradigms All participants completed an at-home 4-week mindfulness training tailored for FM, with the primary goal of training the patients in mindfulness, primarily MM before the combined intervention. The mindfulness intervention comprised 24 sessions—one guided and supervised online 2-hour group session per week through Zoom (maximum 10 participants) and 5 weekly unsupervised guided home-based practices. The weekly components of the brief mindfulness intervention are detailed in Table . The patients monitored their MM and mindfulness routine in a mindfulness diary. The development of the mindfulness intervention was spearheaded by OLGA, an expert mindfulness teacher with more than 10 years’ experience teaching mindfulness, together with PR and FP. The intervention was adapted from the classic mindfulness-based stress reduction program, , with a similar structure to de Moreira et al. The online group sessions in German were carried out by a trained mindfulness facilitator with more than 5 years’ experience teaching meditation. The online group sessions included 3 main aspects—the practice of sitting MM, with the breathing as the object of meditation, mindful activities such as mindfulness eating and walking, and topical education. The goal of the education was to inform the participants about the practice of mindfulness and how it relates to FM (Table ). Participants were encouraged to have an open discussion about their practice and experiences as well as to ask questions to the facilitator. At the end of each group meeting, the participants were instructed to carry out a daily audio-guided MM (20 min) and an informal mindfulness practice of their choice (∼5 min), for example, brushing teeth, walking, and eating. Handouts with the contents of the topic education and the MM recordings were also provided to the participants. Home-based anodal tDCS comprised a constant 2 mA direct electrical current through a pair of saline-saturated 25 cm 2 circular electrodes delivered through a portable battery-driven Sooma tDCS stimulator (Sooma Medical, Helsinki, Finland). Clinic-based anodal tDCS at 2 mA was delivered through a pair of rectangular rubber electrodes (5​​​​​​×7 cm; 35 cm 2 ) by the NeuroConn DC-Stimulator Plus stimulator (NeuroConn, Illmenau, Germany). The anode was placed over the left M1 (C3 according to the 10 to 20 EEG system) and the cathode over the contralateral supraorbital prefrontal cortex (FP2) for both home-based and clinic-based stimulation. For the sham tDCS, the electrodes were placed in the same position as the active stimulation. The previously validated sham protocols – produced an identical indistinguishable sensation to the anodal tDCS. , For the home-based stimulation, patients received prior training in how to operate the device (Fig. ). All combined interventions were supervised by trained investigators and conducted in groups comprising a maximum of 6 participants. At-home combined intervention sessions were supervised by trained personnel through Zoom. Concurrent to the tDCS, a 20-minute audio-guided MM from the last week of the mindfulness training was applied, which focused on the nonjudgmental, nonattached, and present-moment awareness of breathing. , The same MM audio was played daily throughout the combined intervention. Following the 2 weeks of combined intervention, participants continued their daily mindfulness practice until PC4, and were requested to keep a minimum of 3 times of mindfulness practice per week from PC4 to PC12. Defining Clinical Responders Participants rated the German Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire (FIQ; Cronbach α=0.92), a multidimensional measure covering the most relevant symptom domains of FM, at all measurement time points as part of the battery of questionnaires (Fig. ). The FIQ comprises 10 questions relating to the past week. Sum scores range from 0 (no impact of FM) to 100 (maximal impact of FM). The FIQ is widely used in fibromyalgia studies and has been shown to be more sensitive to subjective changes in symptomatology than ratings of pain intensity. We based our definition of responders on an analysis by Bennett et al suggesting a 14% reduction in overall FIQ score to be clinically relevant. To provide evidence for symptom reductions upon MM being associated with improved ER, we defined responders to MM a priori as participants reporting ≥14% reduction in FIQ scores at PM compared with BA (clinical responder at PM). To find out whether participants with clinically relevant symptom reduction have an additional benefit in terms of ER from the combination of MM and active tDCS, a second approach to responder classification was chosen: immediate “add-on” responders to the combination of MM and tDCS were defined as those reporting ≥14% decrease in FIQ at PC0 in comparison to PM (clinical responder at PC0). Description of Questionnaires Used for the Emotion Regulation Composite Score ER is a multidimensional construct referring to people’s deliberate or unconscious efforts to influence one’s own emotions. Although the connection between different strategies of ER and mental health has increasingly become the subject of scientific interest in recent years, a consistent conceptualization is still lacking. Therefore, initially, questionnaires either directly or indirectly operationalizing facets of ER were selected to cover a broad spectrum of possible construct definitions originating from varying theoretical backgrounds, as described below. Interestingly, we found ER target variables from the different assessment instruments to be highly intercorrelated (Fig. ; Cronbach α=0.866). The high internal consistency suggests that all ER target variables selected for the responder analysis appear to measure a similar underlying construct. Consequently, for the main analysis, we integrated the individual ER target variables into an Emotion Regulation Composite Score (ERCS; see statistical analysis for details). In the following section, the theoretical background of the questionnaires used for the assessment of ER is briefly introduced together with their description. Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire (FFMQ) The FFMQ is widely used to assess the effectiveness of MBIS and was constructed based on factor analysis integrating items from 5 independently developed mindfulness questionnaires. The German version of the FFMQ consists of 5 factors: observing (α=0.90), describing (α=0.88), acting with awareness (α=0.74), nonjudgment (α=0.80), and nonreactivity (α=0.78), representing the different facets of mindfulness as it is currently conceptualized. Individual statements mostly address how people deal with their feelings, thoughts, and bodily sensations (eg, “I watch my feelings without getting lost in them”). In total, the FFMQ contains 39 items (8 per subscale, 7 for subscale nonreactivity) that are rated on a 5-point Likert-type scale ranging from 1=“never or very rarely true” to 5=“very often or always true.” For the present analyses, the total summary score of the instrument was used with higher scores indicating a higher level of mindfulness. Psychometric properties (including change sensitivity) of the German version of the FFMQ were shown to be acceptable. Emotion Regulation Skills Questionnaire (ERSQ) The ERSQ comprises 27 items indicative of 9 competencies relevant for successful emotion regulation according to the competence-oriented model of adaptive emotion regulation by Berking and colleagues: attention, clarity, body awareness, understanding, acceptance, resilience, self-support, confrontation, and regulation. Individual statements referring to the past week are rated on a 5-point Likert-type scale ranging from 1=“not at all” to 5=“very often or always true” (eg, “During the past week, I paid attention to my feelings”). As the high internal consistency of the total scale of Cronbach α=0.90 suggests one underlying factor, the total sum score was used with higher values indicating better ER competencies. Volitional Components Inventory (VCI, 52 Items Short Form) On the basis of previous studies highlighting the impact of mindfulness meditation on self-regulation, – the factors self-regulation, self-access, and general life stress were selected from the German version of the 52 items short form of the VCI. , The VCI was constructed against the theoretical framework of Personality Systems Interactions theory assigning a fundamental role to the (intuitive) self-regulation of positive and negative affect for behavioral flexibility during goal pursuit and thus “successful” adaptation to chronic pain. Self-regulation consists of the subscales self-determination, self-soothing, and self-motivation with statements such as “Even when in a state of strong inner tension, I manage to relax.” Self-access comprises the subscales coping with failure, self-awareness, and integrating contradictions with statements such as “When I am in a bad mood, I find it hard to get out of it.” The factor assessing general life stress contains the 2 subscales stress and load (eg, “I must come to terms with huge changes in my life”). Each subscale of the VCI (52 items short form) comprises 4 statements addressing the current situation. The level of agreement is rated on a 4-point Likert-type scale ranging from 1 (not at all) to 4 (fully agree). Higher scores reflect better self-regulation and self-access and higher general life stress. Psychometric properties (including change sensitivity) of the German version of the 52 items short form of the VCI were shown to be acceptable. , Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Scales-21 Items (DASS-21) Convergent to the subscale general life stress of the Volitional Components Inventory, the subscale stress of the German version of the DASS-21 , (Cronbach α=0.82 to 0.87) was used as an indirect measure of the downregulation of negative affect (eg, “I found it difficult to calm down”). The stress subscale comprises 7 statements relating to the past week which are rated on a 4-point Likert-type scale ranging from 0 (did not apply to me at all) to 3 (was very true for me/most of the time true for me) and the sum of the scores for each statement was calculated. Higher scores reflect higher stress levels. Psychometric qualities of the German version of the DASS-21 have been shown to be acceptable. Statistical Analysis Statistical analyses were carried out using SPSS software (IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, version 29.0; IBM Corp, Armonk, NY). Data analyses were blinded to the type of stimulation received (active or sham). Continuous variables are described by mean and SD, ordinal variables by median and interquartile range. Discrete variables are presented as absolute numbers and frequencies. Data are displayed as mean±SD in tables and mean±SEM in figures. All P- values are 2-tailed. Statistical significance was set at P ≤0.05. The respective statistical procedures applied are additionally mentioned in table footnotes and figure legends. Bonferroni multiple testing corrections were performed as indicated there. Before delving into the responder analysis, we first tested the comparability between the treatment groups (MM+active tDCS and MM+active tDCS) at baseline through an unpaired t test for age, clinical status (assessed by the Symptom Severity Index, Widespread Pain Index, and duration of pain), and FIQ scores. A χ 2 test was used to test the comparability of the groups for biological sex. For the intercorrelation pattern of the target variables integrated into the ERCS, pairwise correlations were assessed using Spearman rank correlation coefficient averaged across all measurement time points (BA, PM, PC0, PC4, PC8, PC12). In accordance with the polarity of the majority of target variables, for stress (DASS-21) and general life stress (VCI) polarity was reversed such that higher values represent less stress, reflecting better self-regulatory capacity. The internal consistency averaged across measurement time points was determined by Cronbach alpha reflecting the extent to which the target variables measure aspects of the same latent construct (ie, ER). The ERCS was calculated by averaging z -standardized and equally polarized scores (mindfulness, emotion regulation, self-regulation, self-access, stress, and general life stress) for each measurement time point excluding BA (PM to PC12). To ensure comparability between responders and nonresponders to the MBI at baseline, we conducted an unpaired t test for age, duration of pain, symptom severity index, widespread pain index, ERCS, and the individual variables within the ERCS. A Mann-Whitney U test was employ in case of violation of parametric assumptions. We conducted the same tests to compare the responders and nonresponders to the combined intervention within each intervention group (MM+active tDCS, MM+sham tDCS). To assess differences between responders and nonresponders over time (PM to PC12) with respect to the ERCS and individual target variables, mixed-model ANOVA was selected as statistical procedure due to its popularity and “relative simplicity.” To adjust for baseline scores, linear regression analyses were performed with the ERCS and individual target variables at PM, PC0, PC4, PC8, and PC12 as dependent variables and respective baseline scores as independent variables. Standardized residuals (adjusted for the respective baseline values) were used as dependent variables for mixed-model ANOVA. Assumptions for mixed-model ANOVA were reviewed by explorative data analysis. The Shapiro-Wilk test was used to test for normal distribution. Violations of the normality assumption were detected for the following variables: standardized residuals of ER (ERSQ; PC4) and standardized residuals of self-access (VCI; PC4 and PC8). To account for these, adjunct to the main analyses, analyses of covariance (ANCOVA) of the area under curve (AUC) were conducted, as described below. All remaining variables were normally distributed across measurement time points. Extreme outliers, defined as exceeding three times the interquartile range of a score, could not be identified. The Greenhouse-Geisser adjustment was used to correct for violations from sphericity. Mixed-model ANOVAs were performed with responder status at PM and responder status at PC0 as fixed factors and standardized residuals of the ERCS and individual target scores as dependent variables over time (PM to PC12). For the responder status at PC0, analyses were carried out stratified by tDCS condition (sham vs. active tDCS). Following the recommendations of Leppink et al, main effects were only interpreted in case of insufficient evidence for a group-by-time interaction effect. For group comparisons at each measurement time point, Mann-Whitney U tests were performed (stratified by stimulation group when appropriate). A χ 2 or the Fisher exact tests were used to evaluate stimulation group differences with respect to the frequency of responders and nonresponders. As a complementary approach to mixed-model ANOVA, for analyzing group differences in trajectories of the ERCS, we used the AUC. This approach is widely used in pharmacokinetics and now increasingly being applied with repeated measures designs in psychological and behavioral research. Recent evidence supports that AUC performs comparably to Latent Growth Curve Modeling, especially when dealing with smaller sample sizes. AUC was determined for the ERCS by applying the composite trapezoidal rule for numerical integration. Each trapezoid was calculated by multiplication of length (sum of 2 consecutive ERCS divided by 2) and width (week difference between 2 consecutive measurement time points; eg, ERCS at PC0 minus score at PM) excluding the baseline. Differences between responders and nonresponders with respect to the AUC of the ERCS were determined by one-way ANCOVA with the baseline score as covariate. For both the ANOVAs and ANCOVAs, the effect size was computed as η 2 and was interpreted based on Cohen benchmark categorization (small, η 2 =0.01; medium, η 2 =0.06 and large, η 2 =0.14). To explore the long-term response to the combined intervention with respect to differences in ERCS, clinical responders at PC4 were defined as participants reporting ≥14% improvement in FIQ at PC4 in comparison to PM. The proportion of responders and nonresponders stratified by type of stimulation received were compared by the Fisher exact test. For each intervention group, a mixed model ANOVA (responder status as fixed factor and standardized residuals of ERCS corrected to baseline as dependent variables over time) was conducted to investigate how standardized residuals of ERCS corrected to baseline (dependent variable) changes over time (within-subjects factor) depending on responder status (between-subjects factor). As another exploratory approach to test the response to both the mindfulness training and the combined MM and tDCS intervention, responders to both interventions were defined as participants with responder statuses at both PM and PC0. No statistical analyses were conducted to assess differences in ER comparing responders to both treatment with nonresponders, responders to the brief mindfulness intervention (BMBI) only and responders to combined intervention only due to the low numbers within each group. However, the data was described mathematically. DISCUSSION This study was the first, to our knowledge, to explore the effects of a BMBI tailored for FM and the combination of MM with M1-targeted tDCS on ER in individuals with FM. We found that clinical responders to the 1-month MBI exhibited higher ER competency than nonresponders. This improvement in ER lasted for about 6 weeks. Interestingly, however, the beneficial effect of MM on ER was negated by combining MM and M1-tDCS. A consistent pattern was found for the emotion regulation composite score as well as for the individual ER variables. We observed superior ER competencies in responders who had received a combination of MM and sham M1-tDCS as compared with nonresponders of the same treatment condition. In FM patients who had been randomized to the MM+active M1-tDCS condition, no such group difference depending on responder status could be detected. Moreover, although improvements in ER faded over time, significant group differences between responders and nonresponders in the sham stimulation condition could still be detected at PC12. The rationale for our study was based on the idea to “boost” the effects of MM on brain regions involved in ER by making use of M1 projections to the same circuitry. Unexpectedly, our findings point toward antagonistic neuronal mechanisms underlying M1-targeted tDCS and MM. Contrary to the extensive body of literature addressing mindfulness-based ER, fewer studies have looked into tDCS-induced ER. The main tDCS target was the DLPFC, which plays a central role in ER. While single sessions – or multiple sessions – of anodal DLPFC-tDCS were ineffective in ER in healthy individuals, repeated anodal tDCS of the DLPFC has repeatedly shown positive benefits in ER in patients with FM and depression by improving depressive symptoms. , , , In a recent meta-analysis, stimulation of the prefrontal cortex by repeated anodal tDCS targeting the prefrontal cortex showed positive effects on explicit ER, which entails the voluntary modification of emotional responses, but not on implicit automatic ER compared with controls. No study has yet explored the impact of anodal M1-tDCS on ER strategies. Introduction In the United States, the financial hardship of cancer and its treatments is prevalent and has a profound impact on quality of life for patients and their family members. Over the past decade, financial toxicity , defined as a patient’s problems related to medical costs that may lead to debt and bankruptcy, diminished quality of life, and difficulties accessing medical care, has become accepted as a clinically relevant patient-reported outcome in oncology. The literature largely shows an association of cancer-related financial hardship with increased mortality risk, , elevated biological markers of inflammation, health disparities and poor outcomes, , poor mental health outcomes, , and reduced utilization of available health care. Healthcare providers have an influential role in the experience of financial hardship among their cancer patients. Hong et al’s study of the 2016–2017 Medical Expenditure Panel Survey’s nationally representative data found that cancer patients who reported having a detailed discussion with their providers about cancer care costs, on average, spent 33.8% less on out-of-pocket health care expenses across all age groups with patients ages 18–64 years seeing greater savings (than their older counterparts ages 65+). Even still, cancer patients commonly report unmet needs and dissatisfaction regarding communication with their providers about financial concerns. Moreover, data from our own cancer center points to racial disparities related to unmet financial concerns. Specifically, Kronfli et al’s study (n=266) of patients undergoing radiation therapy with curative intent at our National Cancer Institute (NCI) designated comprehensive cancer center showed that significantly higher proportions of Black versus non-Black patients reported unmet needs regarding pain, stress management, and transportation. Multivariable results showed that Black patients were 2.6, 2.2, 7.2, and 3.4 times more likely than non-Black patients to request assistance with pain, stress, transportation, and financial aid, respectively. Screening and Assessment of Financial Toxicity In 2017, Khera et al’s commentary in Cancer on the financial burden of cancer treatment argued for universal financial distress screening in routine cancer care to be as ubiquitous as psychological distress screening. A provocative challenge at the time that continues to hold. Early and effective screening for financial toxicity in cancer care delivery is critical to equipping clinical teams with information necessary to develop patient-centered interventions that potentially improve patients’ experiences. , Despite mounting evidence on the prevalence of financial hardship, only a small proportion of comprehensive cancer centers utilize financial screening in routine care. A recent study evaluated the implementation of distress management guidelines by 15 of the 18 National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) member institutions. , Findings revealed that only 20% of comprehensive cancer centers screened all patients for psychological distress (including financial hardship) per National Comprehensive Cancer Network guidelines. Extant studies suggest that, due to time constraints and competing demands, oncology providers may rely on their personal clinical judgment and avoid using distress screening tools. – A review of distress screening and management tools in cancer care suggests that initial screening for psychosocial distress should be introduced at the point of entry into cancer care, thus facilitating proper referral to psychosocial oncology specialists for more detailed assessment. Additionally, as patients move along the oncological treatment pathway, serial monitoring of evolving distress associated with practical problems such as financial hardship is necessary because the economic burden of treatments builds up from accumulating treatment costs and likely disruption to occupational engagement related to earned income. According to a recent study of social workers and financial care counselors at a cancer center, barriers to effective utilization of financial resources include frustration over the lack of financial resources, increasingly stringent eligibility criteria, process inefficiencies, limited resources to identify at-risk patients, and inadequate insurance coverage and availability. , It follows that the development of effective and durable strategies to address financial hardship must be informed by patient and community engagement to address these issues. Furthermore, developers must respond to evidence showing that cancer-related financial problems are disproportionately represented by patients who are younger, members of a racial minority group, and have a higher treatment burden, and that these financial problems are found to contribute to cancer patients forgoing or delaying necessary medical care. – Conceptual Frameworks The current study was informed by two conceptual frameworks and one set of guiding principles. First, we used Tucker-Seeley’s expanded conceptual framework of the financial hardship of cancer , as the analytical framework to inform our participant interview guides and to examine the relationships between reported experiences ( ). Based on theories developed to explain health disparities, Tucker-Seeley’s framework of financial hardship after a cancer diagnosis describes experiences occurring within three domains—material, psychosocial, and behavioral—that are situated within the contexts of life course development and occupational culture. Altogether, these aspects may have a bidirectional relationship with a patient’s health outcomes. , This framing also builds upon evidence showing that the measurement of socioeconomic status requires multi-dimensional assessments.

Study Purpose The current research was initiated based on a preliminary interview with the social work team at a National Cancer Institute (NCI) designated comprehensive cancer center located in the dense urban city of Baltimore (University of Maryland Greenebaum Comprehensive Cancer Center). The interview revealed that, between January 1 to April 1, 2020, the social work team received 96 referrals for financial distress from health care providers at the cancer center. Of the 96 patients, only 21 were referred to patient navigation services for help with various treatment-related financial assistance needs. Additionally, the social work team receives an average of 52 patient referrals per month for transportation assistance but does not track whether or how social workers follow-up with these patients. These data suggest that there is some level of screening and referral happening, but no system in place to ensure equitable access among patients. There are currently no clinical processes nor guidelines at the cancer center for systematically identifying patients in need of financial navigation, prioritizing referrals, and offering financial strategies. The purpose of this study is to develop a novel financial navigation pathway that will leverage existing patient financial services and resources with corresponding patient-centered, community-informed strategies, via study participants, that may be utilized in routine care across the cancer care continuum to reduce financial hardship among patients at a National Cancer Institute designated comprehensive cancer center. Our primary research question asks: How can the oncological patient treatment pathway be utilized by the interprofessional care team to reduce cancer-related financial hardship in its material, psychosocial, and behavioral domains? Guidance from this tool centers on utilization of the oncological patient treatment pathway by the interprofessional oncology care team to intervene upon the financial toxicity of cancer. , Throughout this manuscript, the terms financial hardship, financial distress, and financial burden are used interchangeably in reference to challenging experiences with severity that may or may not build to a toxic level-i.e., financial toxicity. Universal Screening for Financial Distress Due to the high volume of patients with financial concerns at the cancer center, the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) Guidelines Version 2.2023 Distress Thermometer and Problem Checklist (Distress Thermometer) will be used to universally screen for financial distress upon initial intake of all cancer patients at the point of entry into the cancer center. The Distress Thermometer screens for financial distress by asking patients to indicate the level of unpleasant experiences they have had in the past week on a scale of 0–10. The tool also contains a problem list that asks patients to indicate any specific concerns by marking all that apply to list of various concerns and provides an open-ended free write option for other concerns. We recommend that Distress Thermometer financial distress screenings be driven and led by a non-physician member of the oncology care team (e.g., physician’s assistant, nurse practitioner, infusion/radiation nurse, etc.) to be assigned according to the workflow of the clinic. Ideally, an electronic version of the Distress Thermometer would be completed by the patient via tablet before or during the first clinic visit, with the option of a paper version or orally administered by a staff member as needed. When possible, follow-up phone calls or tele-visits with the primary oncology team may be advised in lieu of in-person visits to minimize patients’ travel expenses, co-pays, childcare expenses, disruption to work, etc. Since 2015, the American College of Surgeons (ACoS) Commission on Cancer has mandated psychosocial distress screenings for accreditation of cancer centers. According to the National Comprehensive Cancer Network Guidelines Version 2.2023 Distress Management, psychological distress is defined as an emotionally unpleasant psychological (cognitive, behavioral, emotional), social, and/or spiritual experience that may interfere with a patient’s ability to effectively cope with cancer, its physical symptoms, and its treatment. The Distress Thermometer screens for the presence of psychosocial distress among cancer patients. The Distress Thermometer uses a 1-item Likert scale of distress from 0 (no distress) to 10 (extreme distress), with an accompanying list of causes. Recommended Distress Thermometer cutoff scores for detecting distress ranged from 2 to 7, with National Comprehensive Cancer Network guidelines indicating an optimal score of greater than or equal to 4, which varies by the differences in the components that comprise distress. Our investigator team used results from the current study and a comprehensive literature search to discuss and arrive at a recommendation that patients at the cancer center with Distress Thermometer screening results indicating a distress score >4 and >3 practical concerns on the Distress Thermometer problem list be referred by the health care provider who conducted the Distress Thermometer screening to the social work team fora full financial toxicity assessment using the COST-FACIT. Due to the urgency of some financial concerns, we suggest that health care providers make these referrals to the social work team within 3–5 business days of the Distress Thermometer screening. Financial Toxicity Assessment of Vulnerable Patients The COST-FACIT is a standardized patient-reported outcome measure that has been validated to assess financial distress from cancer and its treatments. The COST-FACIT version 2 is a 12-item questionnaire asks patients to respond using a Likert scale. Since its introduction, the COST-FACIT has been shown to provide adequate reliability, validity, and internal consistency for identifying financial distress. Total scores of the COST-FACIT range from 0 to 48 and lower scores relate to higher patient-reported financial toxicity. While there is no established cutoff score with the COST-FACIT, studies have used median scores of 20 or 26 to indicate positive screenings for financial toxicity, while significant financial burden is often indicated by scores less than 22. In addition, Prasad et al’s study stratified gynecologic cancer patients as experiencing either mild (COST-FACIT score, 14–25), moderate (COST-FACIT score, 1–13), or severe (COST-FACIT score, 0) financial toxicity. Our investigator team used results from the current study and a comprehensive literature search to discuss and arrive at procedures for financial toxicity assessment of patients at the cancer center. The COST-FACIT financial toxicity assessment would be led by a social worker who administers the assessment using the same format as the Distress Thermometer. Upon completion, the social worker would document the patients’ COST-FACIT results within the EMR and collaborate with the patient on initiating a relevant financial navigation strategy within 3–5 days of the COST-FACIT assessment. Next steps for financial strategies and a copy of the patients’ COST-FACIT assessment results would be made available to the patient via the electronic patient portal and made available to the referring oncology care provider via the staff electronic portal. The status on the execution of financial strategies would be updated by social workers on an ongoing basis via both the patient and provider electronic portals. Financial Navigation Pathway Although medical financial hardship is not unique to cancer patients, , , the distinct nature of the cancer care continuum calls for interventions that optimize the oncological workflow among the interprofessional care team. Financial navigation of cancer patients is a feasible intervention that is utilized at comprehensive cancers centers across the country to reduce financial hardship. , Service offerings that comprise a financial navigation program vary and may include financial toxicity screening, health insurance optimization, health literacy education, referral to social support services (e.g., housing, transportation, and other health related social needs), as well as financial budgeting and assistance programs. Given this wide range of offerings, an interprofessional approach and concerted collaboration between oncologists, primary care, social workers, and all other members of the interprofessional care team is necessary to arrive at meaningful strategies for the patient population at the cancer center. presents the financial navigation pathway for cancer patients at a National Cancer Institute designated comprehensive cancer center

Across this financial navigation pathway, mapping the appropriate timing of financial strategies and ensuring consistent and timely communication among the interprofessional care team is essential. Anticipatory guidance from cancer care professionals is warranted and strongly desired among patient participants who struggled with the financial consequences of cancer, and even more so among patients who reported pre-existing low income prior to their cancer diagnosis. Informed by these results, extant evidence, and clinical experience, qualified members of our research team in the current study recommend specific strategies for intervening upon each of these themes of financial hardship and the timing of these interventions along the cancer care continuum. Thus, the current study derived patient-centered, community-informed strategies from cancer patients and cancer care professionals to inform a sustainable financial navigation pathway for routine screening and intervention to reduce financial toxicity across the cancer care continuum at an NCI designated comprehensive cancer center ( ). Practice Implications Due to the strain of the global pandemic and post-pandemic consequences, cancer center staff have shared experiences of great shortfalls in staff capacity attributed to high turnover, burnout, and vacant positions. Given these significant challenges, the resulting financial navigation pathway may require practical adjustments to triage patients with the most severe needs and ensure that staff members at the cancer center have the capacity to sufficiently respond. Even with the potential need for more modest interim goals, the cancer center’s staff, patients, and their supporters will all benefit from a transparent process of financial navigation. When adjusting to reflect reduced staff capacity, two areas for customization to ensure patient referrals of those with the greatest needs is in our recommendations for financial distress screening and financial toxicity assessment across the financial navigation pathway. Specifically, we suggest that Distress Thermometer screenings with scores of >4 be referred to social work for a financial toxicity assessment. This Distress Thermometer cutoff score for referrals may be adjusted higher to respond to the current staff capacity. Similarly, we suggest that patients who score <20 on the COST-FACT receive more frequent re-assessment with patients scoring <15 to be re-assessed in 3 months while patients scoring 20–15 be re-assessed in 6 months. We also advise that all patients referred for financial toxicity assessment be re-assessed on a yearly basis at minimum. The recommended COST-FACIT cutoff scores and corresponding frequency of re-assessments may be adjusted according to patient needs and staff capacity of the clinic environment. Accordingly, patients experiencing the highest toxicity would be prioritized, and staff would be more likely to fully execute the suggested financial strategies at each re-assessment. Communication and collaboration on staff roles and responsibility across the interdisciplinary care team is critical to the effectiveness of the financial navigation pathway. In the setting of a busy clinical practice, responsibilities that are workflow driven are more likely to be completed, and tasks that can be completed by qualified non-physician staff should be assigned accordingly. We recommend that screening for financial hardship be led by a non-physician member of the primary oncology care team (e.g., physician’s assistant, nurse practitioner, infusion/radiation nurse, etc.), who then makes referrals to social work for a full financial toxicity assessment. The specific staff assigned to this leadership role may be further narrowed or adjusted to reflect the staffing of the cancer center and optimize efficiency. Equally important, the social work team must establish and monitor their capacity for responding to referrals. For example, we estimate that one full-time social worker at our cancer center has a weekly capacity to manage 6–9 patient referrals for financial toxicity assessment and subsequent financial navigation when considering the intensity of unmet needs among patients at our cancer center located in a dense urban setting. Staff workload can also be reduced by electronically administering re-assessments of either the Distress Thermometer screening or COST-FACIT financial toxicity assessment, since both are self-administered tools in which patients respond to questions independently. Staff workload can also be reduced by electronically administering re-assessments of either the Distress Thermometer screening or COST-FACIT financial toxicity assessment, since both are self-administered tools in which patients respond to questions independently. Limitations and Strengths This study had limitations. Cancer patients who were interviewed in the study were treated at a National Cancer Institute designated comprehensive cancer center, which provided insights into the experiences of financial hardship for those who were able to access care. It does, however, exclude the perspectives of those who live within the cancer center’s catchment area, but are unable to access the cancer center and/or other medical care. It would have been helpful to include these patients not receiving care at the cancer center to examine potential barriers to accessing necessary medical care and their associations with financial toxicity. Another limitation is that most patients (71 %) participating in this study were diagnosed with breast cancer and had curable disease that did not require chemotherapy. Also, over half of patient participants (54%) in our study held college or graduate degrees and reported incomes above this region’s median income of $54,124 between 2017–2021, The combination of lower disease burden, higher education attainment, and higher income levels suggest that we may have missed important aspect of financial toxicity from patients with severe needs. Notwithstanding, these limitations are outweighed by our study’s strengths. This study makes a novel contribution to knowledge on patient-centered and community-informed approaches to developing a useful practice tool that can help cancer care providers to reduce the financial hardship of cancer experienced by patients in their care by leveraging existing services, resources, and interprofessional collaboration. The resulting financial navigation pathway establishes a systematic standard of care that creates equitable access to resources and strategies aimed at reducing the financial toxicity of cancer. By suggesting strategies that respond directly to the experiences and concerns expressed by cancer patients and cancer care professionals and optimizing the oncological workflow, we developed a tool that can be tested for effectiveness with a random sample of participants that could potentially address some of the limitations mentioned above. Conclusions This study followed an innovative approach of centering the experiences of cancer patients and input from their care professionals to construct a financial navigation pathway tool that can be used in routine care at a National Cancer Institute designated comprehensive cancer center. Findings are a necessary first step toward developing a sustainable approach to reduce financial toxicity among cancer patients. It is the first in-depth investigation of patient-centered, community-informed financial navigation strategies at this NCI-designated comprehensive cancer center located in a dense urban area. Future research is needed to test the structures, processes, and outcomes of the financial navigation pathway tool; examine its impact on financial toxicity, and health-related outcomes; as well as better understand how much navigation is needed to bring about meaningful change.

This AHRQ toolkit, based on the CANDOR process, is intended to assist hospitals in implementing communication and optimal resolution programs. A traditional approach when unexpected harm occurs often follows a "deny-and-defend" strategy, providing limited information to patients and families, and avoiding admission of fault. All Rights Reserved. 2026 Background: Professionalism is a core competency in graduate medical education, yet research examining specialty-specific professionalism perceptions between trainees and faculty remains limited, particularly regarding the influence of role and institutional culture on these perceptions. This study examined how anesthesiology trainees and attendings perceive unprofessional behavior and whether these perceptions differ based on participant characteristics. Methods: A multisite cross-sectional survey was conducted at five anesthesiology residency programs from February to March 2024. Participants rated degree of unprofessionalism on 19 workplace vignettes depicting potentially unprofessional behaviors using a 7-point Likert scale. Vignettes were categorized into five themes: verbal, supervision, quality, time, and engagement. Proportional odds models examined differences in ratings based on role (trainee vs . attending), adjusting for gender, race, underrepresented status, and institution. Results: Among 369 respondents (153 trainees, 216 attendings; 35.9% response rate), perceptions varied by scenario and participant characteristics. Six vignettes were more consistently rated as unprofessional (more than 80% unprofessional ratings), while four showed higher variability (less than 50% unprofessional ratings). Significant institutional differences were observed in five vignettes (odds ratios [ORs] less than 0.14 or greater than 3.7; P < 0.0001 to 0.027). Age influenced ratings of five vignettes (ORs, 0.75, 1.68, 1.63, 1.35, and 1.31, respectively; P < 0.0001 to 0.027), while gender, race, and underrepresented status showed no significant differences. After adjustment for demographics, trainees and attendings differed significantly in their ratings of 10 vignettes ( P < 0.0001 to 0.033). Attendings rated nine scenarios as more unprofessional than trainees (ORs ranging from 0.26 to 0.50), while trainees rated only one scenario as more unprofessional than attendings (OR, 2.01). Conclusions: Perceptions of unprofessional behavior among anesthesiology professionals vary significantly by role and institution. These findings underscore the importance of context-sensitive approaches to professionalism education that acknowledge diverse perspectives and institutional cultures while maintaining core professional standards. In a survey of 369 respondents across five anesthesia departments who were asked to review 19 hypothetical vignettes, perceptions of professionalism varied by hospital and participant characteristics, with attendings more likely than residents to characterize behavior described in a given vignette as being unprofessional.
